title: South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc., 585 U.S. 162 (2018): syllabus, majority opinion and dissent (text hosted by Cornell LII)

history.reason: Source read directly on the access date; findings transcribed from the document.

publisher: U.S. Supreme Court (text as hosted by Cornell Legal Information Institute)
source_type: Court opinion (hosted copy of official text)
reliability: Primary legal text, but read through a university-hosted copy, not supremecourt.gov (the supremecourt.gov PDF URL tried returned 404). Opinion authors are judges deciding a dispute, not measuring seller burden; the burden statements are judicial reasoning and a dissent citing a GAO report.
findings: Decided June 21, 2018 (argued April 17, 2018); the Court overruled Quill Corp. v. North Dakota and National Bellas Hess v. Illinois, which had barred states from requiring out-of-state sellers without physical presence to collect sales tax.
The South Dakota Act covers sellers that deliver more than $100,000 of goods or services into the state or engage in 200 or more separate transactions annually, and is not retroactive.

The majority acknowledges burdens "may pose legitimate concerns in some instances, particularly for small businesses that make a small volume of sales to customers in many States", and says software "may make it easier" for them to cope, possibly soon, and that Congress may legislate.

The majority notes South Dakota is a Streamlined Sales and Use Tax Agreement member, which provides sellers access to state-paid sales tax administration software, with audit immunity for sellers who use it.

The dissent (Roberts, C.J., joined by three Justices) states that over 10,000 jurisdictions levy sales taxes with differing rates, exemptions and product definitions (citing the GAO Sales Taxes report GAO-18-114, Nov. 2017), and that correct calculation and remittance will likely prove baffling for many retailers.
The dissent cites estimates that the old rule cost states between $8 and $33 billion per year in revenue (GAO $8 to $13 billion; petitioner cites $23 and $33.9 billion).
limitations: Hosted copy on a third-party site; page text was extracted from HTML and quotes were checked against it, but not against the supremecourt.gov PDF.
The 10,000 jurisdictions figure and the revenue estimates are secondhand (dissent quoting GAO and briefs); the GAO report itself was not read (gao.gov not accessed).
Describes 2018 conditions; says nothing on current thresholds, tooling or measured compliance cost.
